headline: Protecting Primates Could Save Thousands of Other Species
meta_description: A new study shows that safeguarding primate habitats can protect vast ecosystems. Protecting just 30% of Yunnan could shield 86% of threatened animals.
summary_short: Scientists discovered that primates could be powerful umbrella species for conservation. Protecting their habitats saves thousands of other animals and plants too.
body:
A 2025 study has revealed an elegant solution hiding in plain sight: save the homes of primates, and you'll protect thousands of other species simultaneously. Researchers analyzing 16 primate species across China's Yunnan province found that if just 30% of the region were designated a primate conservation priority area, 86% of the threatened and endemic mammals, amphibians, birds and reptiles would have about a third of their habitats protected. The same effort would shield 72% of the seed plants found there, plus more than half of the province's annual carbon storage.

For decades, conservation has focused on iconic umbrella species like tigers and giant pandas—animals whose habitat needs are so vast that protecting them safeguards entire ecosystems. This study suggests primates deserve the same status. These charismatic animals require large tracts of healthy forest to survive, and by securing those territories, countless other wildlife living in the same ecosystem benefit automatically.

The approach is already gaining traction globally. The nonprofit Rainforest Trust is protecting habitats of critically endangered Grauer's gorillas in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which will help safeguard more than 11,000 species. Similarly, protecting Bornean orangutans could secure an estimated 20,000 species across the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. What makes primates particularly effective as conservation flagships is their charisma—they inspire both funding and public advocacy in ways that quieter species cannot. Yet beyond their appeal, primates play vital ecological roles: they disperse seeds through their diet and serve as prey for larger predators. When forests decline, experts note, primates often disappear first, signaling deeper ecosystem damage. The umbrella approach, conservationists say, is practical and powerful—limited mainly by human governance and commitment, not by the concept itself.
quick_facts: Protecting 30% of Yunnan for primates could protect 86% of threatened animals
Study analyzed 16 primate species across China's biodiverse Yunnan province
Grauer's gorillas in Congo protect habitats of over 11,000 species
Bornean orangutan conservation could shield estimated 20,000 species
2025 study shows primates are effective umbrella species for ecosystems
